content: Tinea versicolor, also known as pityriasis versicolor, is a common fungal skin infection caused by the yeast Malassezia furfur (previously referred to as Pityrosporum ovale). This yeast is a normal component of the skin's microbiota but can become pathogenic under specific conditions, such as in warm and humid environments. The clinical presentation of tinea versicolor includes oval or irregularly shaped spots that range in size from 1/4 to 1 inch in diameter. These spots often coalesce to form larger patches. The affected areas may exhibit fine scaling, which appears as a superficial, ash-like layer on the skin. The lesions can vary in color, appearing pale, dark tan, or pink, often with a reddish undertone. The discoloration may darken when the patient becomes overheated, such as during a hot shower or after physical activity. The borders of the lesions are typically well-defined. The most commonly affected areas include the back, underarms, upper arms, chest, lower legs, and neck. In some cases, the face may also be involved. Under microscopic examination, the yeast within the lesions often displays a characteristic spaghetti and meatball appearance, with round yeast cells and filamentous hyphae. In individuals with darker skin tones, hypopigmentation (loss of skin color) is frequently observed, whereas those with lighter skin tones may experience hyperpigmentation (increased skin color). These pigmentary changes have led to the colloquial term sun fungus for this condition. The diagnosis of tinea versicolor is primarily clinical, based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions. Microscopic examination of skin scrapings can confirm the diagnosis by revealing the typical fungal morphology. Tinea versicolor must be distinguished from other dermatological conditions that present with erythematous, scaly, annular, and pruritic rashes. Differential diagnoses include other fungal infections, eczema, psoriasis, and seborrheic dermatitis. The prevalence of tinea versicolor is relatively high, affecting an estimated 2% to 8% of the population in the United States. It is most commonly seen in adolescents and young adults, particularly in warm and humid climates. The yeast thrives on skin lipids and dead skin cells, which contribute to its proliferation. Treatment options for tinea versicolor include both topical and systemic antifungal therapies. Topical treatments are often the first line of therapy and include: Selenium sulfide 2.5% (e.g., Selsun® shampoo in the UK, though not Selsun Blue, which contains only 1%) or ketoconazole 2% (e.g., Nizoral® ointment or shampoo). These are applied to dry skin, left on for 10 minutes, and then washed off. This regimen is repeated daily for two weeks. Other topical antifungal agents, such as clotrimazole, miconazole, or terbinafine, may also be used, though they are less commonly recommended. Hydrogen peroxide has been reported to alleviate symptoms and, in some cases, resolve the condition. Systemic antifungal treatments are reserved for more extensive or recurrent cases and include: Ketoconazole 400 mg orally as a single dose, or 200 mg daily for seven days. Fluconazole 400 mg orally as a single dose. Itraconazole 400 mg orally daily for three to seven days. For single-dose regimens, efficacy can be enhanced by inducing sweating through exercise 1-2 hours after taking the medication. The sweat is allowed to evaporate, and the patient is advised to delay showering for 24 hours, leaving a film of the medication on the skin. Recurrence of tinea versicolor is common. The preferred antimicrobial regimen for tinea versicolor includes: Ketoconazole 400 mg orally as a single dose, or 200 mg daily for seven days, or 2% cream applied once daily for two weeks. Alternative regimens include fluconazole 400 mg orally as a single dose or itraconazole 400 mg orally daily for three to seven days.
